Hout Bay Fire

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Thousands left homeless in massive fire

Summary:
We tend to do stories on massive fires which take away properties of people whose insurance can generally make right but every now and again a tragic fire sweeps through settlements destroying people's homes and taking life and I think the story of the Hout Bay fire which has left thousands homeless and 2 people dead raises many questions and also shows hope. The hope is how the community of Hout Bay is galvanizing themselves to assist the thousands of displaces residents. There are some sinister elements to this story and that can be told by a photographer who saw, during the midst of the fire, fire engines being stoned and also hose pipes being cut. Why? What motivates this behaviour? There are further questions we ask: These informal settlements always present a tragedy awaiting to happen. What is the solution? Is there anything practically that could be done now? Secondly we can portray some examples of designs for shacks or fire repellants that could be used for the future. Why have these not been used? One is a fire resistant paint but this apparently is very expensive. We will also show video footage of an experiment where it takes exactly 40 seconds for a shack to be engulfed in flames after a candle has fallen over and lit something. This is story is also about how unless we are able to provide proper housing with wide enough alleys between them, these terrible fires will keep happening.

Moreover, this is a story of a community galvanized to help each other.

Press Release:


Cape Town fires
As Cape Town battles drought and extreme temperatures, strong winds added to the devastation when fires broke out in informal settlements around the city, leaving thousands homeless. A massive relief effort by City of Cape Town disaster management and NGOs has been established to assist those affected…but until living conditions change drastically, these informal settlements are ticking time bombs.


Script:


Three deadly fires in cape town last weekend which claimed 10 lives once again showed just how venerable informal settlements are. The worst of the three fires took place in the Houtbay, in the township of Imizamo yethu an informal settlement of 30 000 inhabitants, located, on the hill overlooking the valley.

It started in the early hours of Saturday morning on the upper slopes. Strong gusting winds spread the fire quickly and consumed every shack in its path. Senior fireman Brandon Rhodes knew WHAT HE WAS IN FOR.

Brandon Rhodes: Most important is to actually stop the spread of the fire and that is what we do as firefighters. We try and stop it especially because if you don’t stop the spread of the fire the next shack is going and the next shack and you find it is rolling and you chasing after a fire.

As each shack went up in flames, the panic increased. Some residents even flattened shacks to create firebreak.

Justin Sullivan: You know people were screaming, people were crying, people were helping children, helping animals. Every 20 seconds a gad bottle was exploding so it kind of felt like I was in a war zone and it was just absolute panic. Nothing I have ever experienced before.

Photographer Justin Sullivan was on the scene where he alternated between assisting panicking residents and capturing the grief.

Justin: It was completely heart wrenching to see what was going on, you've always seen these in the news, you’ve seen pictures, you've heard stories and I couldn’t wrap my head around what was going on.

The fire would continue to rage for 20 hours. Hampering the firefighting efforts was that the narrow access roads were filled with fleeing residents who were desperate to save their belongings., which often lay strewn access the the roadside.

LINK: Despite the desperation of the community here and the very urgent need to bring the flames under control, there were reports that a number of firefighters were threatened, that their fire trucks were stoned and that water hoses were cut.

That was the experience of Brandon Rhodes.

Brandon: We were literally being threatened. You literally being pushed around, you being threatened, you not doing your job. You hearing people say they want tot throw ricks at you. They want to attack you and you could see the atmosphere was difficult.

Welcome Witbooi: Everybody is confused. People do not know how to respond.

Welcome Witbooi who worlds closely with the community understood the frustration of residents – they could not understand why a fire truck would pass by their burning homes.

Welcome: So they would have to pass the area where it is burned to basically stop it there but people don’t understand that because they have not been educated so they thing that the fire, the fire fighters are actually passing their house and not thinking about helping them later on.
Justin: The hoses that I did see who were in the hands of the local community were just so panic stricken they were just trying to get water on the houses. So they were attempting to cut them, to break them to break them apart, just to try and save those houses.

And adding to the tension were language barriers.

Brandon: I don’t speak Xhosa and you also get the foreigners. They speak a different language so communicating is a big problem when you telling them this is what you trying to do.

Early Saturday evening, the fire was finally put out, a leaving shaken and traumatized community to count the cost.

4 died in the blaze., just under 2000 homes destroyed and 10 000 residents displaced, like Benson mwale. He rushed home from work when he heard about the fire but He was unable to save anything.

Benson: All my stuff inside. All my stuff which is there because I was not able to come and rescue everything because the fire was very hot you know. So I wasn’t able to come inside to take my stuff. So everything was gone.

Benson Mwale who lives here with his wife and child will have to rebuild.

Benson: I don’t have anything to say you know. To start again is very tough you know. It is very tough to start again.

LINK: In the immediate aftermath of the fire, dozens of organizations and private individuals across cape town and beyond were galvanized into lending a hand.

Local residents and volunteers from around the cape pitched in. supplies from businesses and individuals streamed in to assist the 1000s of resident many of whom were left with nothing. On Tuesday they queued at a local field where a command center had been set up. After registering, they started to receive much needed supplies. It was a massive logistical operation.

Directing operation on the field was graham Bradford.

Graham: We just volunteered to help coordinate this. There has been like over 200 volunteers and its needed quite a lot of coordination.
Lebogang: People are just coming through and saying where can I be of assistance. So its not even about the organization, its just about people coming forward and saying can I help.

Even pupils like Yolanda took of school to lend a hand.

Yolanda: I am here because I want to bring back to my community by doing all that it needed so I am providing a hand where there is a need which is thee are clothes and items which are donated here.

Joanne: This is the biggest disaster hout bay has seen on a humanitarian level for the last 26 years.

Joanne chemaly heads up a disaster relief origination called thula thula houtbay. She started it in response to the many previous fires in informal settlements in the valley.

Joanne: I just can’t believe what the community, what volunteers, the retailers the hout bay residents. People from all over cape town, corporates, massive corporates have just come up and said " What do you need?"

Immediately after the fire, the city’s disaster management team swung into action. A massive clean up operation started and its still is going. The city also provides free building materials to any community which had suffered a fire.

LINK: This wasn’t the first fire to have swept through this area and it probably wont be the last but in an astonishing show of resilience, the rebuilding process has already started.

Almost immediately structures started going up again as residents raced to create a home for themselves and their families.

Xanthea: Many of them had a few possessions left and belongings which they wanted to protect and guard and they also wanted to safe guard their site.

But the city wants to use the opportunity of making this area safer by reblocking it, and after negotiating with the community, the building of houses stopped briefly.

Xanthea: The plan is to reblock the area. Create what we call superblocks which is just reblocking at a larger scale. We will provide access ways because their is very limited access to that part of the community and we will also put in pedestrian walk ways. We will provide water and sanitation at the periphery of the superblocks and bring in legal electrification pint for every single household within that superblock.

Community leader samkelo krweqe is however not holding his breath.

Samkelo: Because every time we get fire, city officials, the government itself run down here promising. We going to be doing this we going to be doing that. As soon as everything settles down, they give you your material, they vanish.

He says that this type of intervention is long overdue.

Samkelo: You cannot believe that these people live here for the past 13-16 years. They do not have electricity, if they need to go fetch water, they must walk 500m to 1km to go fetch water.

The city can only start revamping the area once its been cleared –and temporary tents have been provided. However, the community is continuing with building of their homes and the city is now threatening to dismantle them. It’s a tense time.

The over a 100 million rand the city says it will be spending on the upgrade of the township could prevent further fires here. Its all about prevention, says Welcome Witbooi, He wants every structure painted with fire retardant paint buts its expensive. He has been involved in several community projects where this paint has been applied and tested including in an area of Imizamo Yethu – with amazing results.

Welcome: You will see that most of the shacks are painted with color and this paint prevents fires and it has been applied a half and a half ago and since the application of this paint no fires have struck the z section of IY

The upgrade of this community might prevent fires, but will have come too ate for those who lost their lives in it.

Xanthea: And so we hoping as a city we can use this particular situation as tragic as it is, to try and really rebuild a different Imizano Yethu,
